lessonTitle: Neurodegenerative and Neuromuscular Disease: Parkinson Disease, Dementia and Delirium, GBS, MS and Myasthenia

blocks.text: A retired joiner is told by his wife that he has stopped swinging his right arm when he walks, his handwriting has become tiny and his voice has gone quiet. Elsewhere in the clinic a young woman complains that her drooping eyelids and double vision get worse by evening and improve after rest. Different structures fail in each, but the pattern of symptoms points to the lesion.

blocks.markdown: The nervous system is vulnerable when neurones degenerate (Parkinson disease, dementia), when myelin is attacked (multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome) or when transmission at the neuromuscular junction fails (myasthenia gravis). Localisation is the key skill: upper versus lower motor neurone signs, central versus peripheral lesion, and the time course (acute, relapsing-remitting, progressive) together suggest the disease.

blocks.title: Parkinson disease
blocks.text: Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with intraneuronal alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies). Diagnosis requires bradykinesia (slowness with decrement of amplitude or speed) plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical features of Parkinson disease.** Motor: asymmetric 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor, bradykinesia (small handwriting, reduced blinking, hypomimia, soft voice), lead-pipe rigidity with cogwheeling, stooped posture, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing and later postural instability. Non-motor features may precede motor signs by years: loss of smell, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, and later dementia and autonomic failure. **Treatment principles** are symptomatic: replace dopamine with levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) to prevent peripheral conversion and nausea; alternatives or adjuncts are dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and COMT inhibitors. Long-term levodopa causes motor fluctuations (wearing-off) and dyskinesias. Avoid dopamine antagonists (haloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine); domperidone, which does not cross the blood-brain barrier, is the preferred antiemetic. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy matter, and deep brain stimulation is an option for selected patients.

rows: Early episodic memory loss, then language and visuospatial decline
Well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep disorder, neuroleptic sensitivity
Inattention, disorganised thinking, altered consciousness; often hallucinations
Amyloid plaques, tau tangles, medial temporal atrophy
Acute illness: infection, drugs, metabolic, retention, pain
blocks.caption: Common causes of dementia compared with delirium.

blocks.title: Delirium is a medical emergency
blocks.text: Delirium is acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention, caused by a physical illness, and it is distinct from dementia although dementia is the commonest risk factor. Look for infection, drugs (especially anticholinergics and opioids), electrolyte disturbance, urinary retention, constipation and pain, and treat the cause.

blocks.title: Dementia or delirium?
blocks.prompt: An 82-year-old woman with mild memory problems for 3 years became drowsy and agitated over 2 days, picking at the bedclothes and seeing people in the room. She has a temperature of 38.2 degrees C and a positive urine dipstick. Which is the dominant diagnosis?

steps.text: Time course: three years of mild memory loss suggests underlying dementia, but the change over two days is acute.
Attention and consciousness: drowsiness and agitation with visual misperceptions and inattention fluctuating through the day are features of delirium.
Cause: fever and urinary infection are plausible precipitants. Treat the infection, hydrate, review drugs and reorient the patient.

blocks.answer: Delirium superimposed on probable dementia, precipitated by infection.

rows: Acute ascending symmetrical weakness and areflexia over days to 4 weeks, often 1 to 3 weeks after infection (such as Campylobacter); autonomic instability, respiratory failure
CSF protein raised with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation); nerve conduction shows demyelination
IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; monitor forced vital capacity and ECG
Relapsing and remitting episodes separated in time and space: optic neuritis, brainstem signs (internuclear ophthalmoplegia), myelopathy, Lhermitte sign; young adults, more in women
MRI periventricular and spinal cord lesions; oligoclonal bands in CSF
High-dose methylprednisolone for relapse; disease-modifying therapy to reduce relapses
Fatigable weakness: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness worsening with use and by evening
Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (or anti-MuSK); decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; CT chest for thymoma
Pyridostigmine; immunosuppression; thymectomy in selected patients
blocks.caption: Recognising GBS, MS and myasthenia gravis.
Bedside monitoring of respiratory muscle weakness in GBS or myasthenic crisis.

blocks.title: Watching the respiratory muscles
blocks.prompt: A patient with GBS weighing 80 kg has FVC 2.0 L today, down from 3.2 L yesterday. A commonly used warning level is an FVC below 20 mL/kg. Calculate the FVC per kg and interpret it.

steps.text: Convert litres to millilitres: 2.0 L = 2000 mL.
25 mL/kg is above 20 mL/kg, but a fall of about 40% in a day is a worrying trend, so repeat the measurement frequently and alert intensive care.

blocks.answer: 25 mL/kg: above the warning threshold but falling fast, so monitor closely.

items: Parkinsonism with early falls, vertical gaze palsy or autonomic failure suggests an atypical syndrome such as progressive supranuclear palsy or multiple system atrophy.

Myasthenic crisis (respiratory weakness) can be precipitated by infection and drugs (aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers); treat with IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange and ventilatory support.
In GBS, do not use steroids; IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange are effective.
A first demyelinating episode (optic neuritis) with MRI lesions disseminated in space and time supports MS.
Cholinesterase inhibitors benefit Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia, and antipsychotics should be avoided in Lewy body dementia.

points: Parkinson disease is nigral dopaminergic loss causing bradykinesia, rest tremor and rigidity, treated with levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor; dopamine antagonists must be avoided.
Dementia is chronic and progressive; delirium is acute, fluctuating and caused by acute illness. Lewy body dementia combines fluctuation, hallucinations and parkinsonism.
GBS is acute ascending demyelinating weakness with areflexia and raised CSF protein; monitor vital capacity.
MS is relapsing CNS demyelination disseminated in time and space; myasthenia is fatigable weakness from antibodies at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a unilateral pill-rolling rest tremor, slow movements, cogwheel rigidity and a stooped posture. Which pathological change underlies his condition?

options.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Loss of cholinergic neurones in the hippocampus alone

questions.correctOptionText: Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the basis of Parkinson disease.
distractorRationale.b: Hippocampal cholinergic loss relates to Alzheimer disease.
distractorRationale.d: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis.

questions.explanation: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia circuits and causes bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor. Lewy bodies containing alpha-synuclein are the characteristic histology.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease is admitted with vomiting and a chest infection. Which antiemetic should be avoided?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is a central dopamine antagonist that worsens parkinsonism.
distractorRationale.b: Domperidone does not cross the blood-brain barrier appreciably.
distractorRationale.c: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist, not a dopamine antagonist.
distractorRationale.d: Cyclizine is an antihistamine and is not a dopamine antagonist.

questions.explanation: Central dopamine antagonists block the already depleted dopamine signalling and can precipitate severe rigidity. Domperidone is peripherally acting and is the preferred antiemetic in Parkinson disease.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man has memory problems that fluctuate from day to day, vivid well-formed visual hallucinations of children, mild parkinsonism, and became rigid and unresponsive after haloperidol. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and neuroleptic sensitivity.
distractorRationale.b: Alzheimer disease features early episodic memory loss without these.
distractorRationale.c: Vascular dementia is stepwise with focal signs.
distractorRationale.d: Frontotemporal dementia causes behaviour or language change.

questions.explanation: Fluctuating cognition with recurrent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism is the core triad of Lewy body dementia. Severe sensitivity to antipsychotics is a supportive feature and these drugs should be avoided.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman with a urinary tract infection becomes confused over 36 hours. She is drowsy by day, cannot sustain attention, and has been picking at the bedclothes. What is the most appropriate description of her condition?

options.text: Delirium, to be treated by finding and treating the cause

questions.correctOptionText: Delirium, to be treated by finding and treating the cause

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acute onset, fluctuation and inattention with an infection.
distractorRationale.b: Alzheimer disease is gradual and attention is preserved early.
distractorRationale.c: Vascular dementia is stepwise, not a 36-hour illness.
distractorRationale.d: Acute confusion is never normal ageing.

questions.explanation: Delirium is defined by acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness, and is a marker of acute physical illness. Management is to treat the infection and other contributors and use non-pharmacological supportive measures.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman had a week of painful loss of vision in one eye that recovered, and now has a 3-week episode of numbness in the legs with an electric shock sensation on neck flexion. MRI shows periventricular lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: episodes separated in time and space with periventricular lesions.
distractorRationale.b: GBS is a single acute ascending peripheral neuropathy.
distractorRationale.c: Myasthenia gives fatigable weakness, not sensory episodes.
distractorRationale.d: Parkinson disease is progressive and unrelated.

questions.explanation: Optic neuritis and then a spinal cord episode, separated in time and space, with Lhermitte sign and periventricular MRI lesions, are classic for relapsing-remitting MS. This is CNS demyelination.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome has an FVC of 1.2 L. Calculate the FVC in mL/kg (a value below 20 mL/kg is a warning sign for ventilatory failure).
questions.explanation: FVC = 1200 mL / 70 kg = 17.1 mL/kg, which is below 20 mL/kg. This patient needs immediate review for ventilatory support, and treatment with IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.

questions.stem: A woman with myasthenia gravis in suspected crisis has FVC 1.9 L. Her predicted FVC is 4.75 L. Calculate the FVC as a percentage of predicted.
questions.explanation: 1.9 / 4.75 x 100 = 40% of predicted. This marked reduction reflects respiratory muscle weakness and warrants urgent critical care review and treatment with plasma exchange or immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: Describe the clinical features of Parkinson disease and the principles of its drug treatment.
markingGuide: Bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity
Asymmetric onset, stooped posture, shuffling gait, hypomimia, micrographia
Non-motor: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, later dementia and autonomic failure
Pathology: nigral dopaminergic loss with Lewy bodies
Levodopa with carbidopa or benserazide as first-line symptomatic treatment
Alternatives or adjuncts: dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors
questions.explanation: The motor features follow loss of nigrostriatal dopamine, so treatment replaces dopamine, and long-term levodopa causes fluctuations. Drugs that block dopamine worsen symptoms and must be avoided.

questions.stem: Compare the typical presentation and key investigations of Guillain-Barre syndrome, multiple sclerosis and myasthenia gravis.
markingGuide: GBS: acute ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia after infection
GBS: CSF protein raised with normal cells; demyelination on nerve conduction; monitor FVC; IVIG or plasma exchange
MS: relapsing-remitting CNS episodes (optic neuritis, brainstem, spinal cord), separated in time and space
MS: periventricular lesions on MRI; oligoclonal bands
Myasthenia: fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia, bulbar symptoms worse with use
Myasthenia: anti-AChR antibodies, CT thymus; pyridostigmine and immunosuppression
Distinguishes central versus peripheral versus neuromuscular junction
questions.explanation: Each condition targets a different site: peripheral myelin, central myelin and the neuromuscular junction. The time course and the pattern of weakness point to the diagnosis, with antibodies, MRI and CSF or nerve studies confirming it.

questions.stem: True or false: delirium is characterised by insidious onset over years with preserved attention and a stable level of consciousness.
questions.explanation: Delirium has an acute onset over hours to days, fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness. The description given is closer to Alzheimer disease.
